extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, readers, and authors of narrative (non-systematic) medical review articles
extracted.subtask_description: A brief, six-item critical appraisal instrument (SANRA) for evaluating the methodological and reporting quality of non-systematic/narrative review articles in medicine. Each item is scored 0 (low) to 2 (high) and the sum (0–12) indicates overall quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1: Explanation of the review’s importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript should explain the importance of the review topic (why the topic matters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor definitions and examples are provided in the SANRA 'explanations and instructions' document to guide rating. Raters sometimes disagreed on this item; training is recommended. Score 0–2 (0 = low standard, 1 = intermediate, 2 = high standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2: Statement of aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The review should state clear aims (what the review intends to address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided anchor definitions/examples when judging clarity and appropriateness of aims. Score 0–2. Raters often agreed on this item (high single-item agreement reported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 3: Description of the literature search
rubrics_metrics.description: The manuscript should describe its literature search (how the authors identified relevant literature; note: narrative reviews are not expected to be fully systematic, but search methods should be described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate completeness and transparency of the search description using anchors. This item tended to score lower in field tests. Score 0–2. The scale is intended for non-systematic reviews—'systematic' implies explicit search methods; SANRA evaluates whether search methods are described even if non-systematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 4: Referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: References should be adequate and appropriate (accurate citation of relevant literature and appropriate use of references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether referencing is comprehensive, balanced, and correctly presented. Raters disagreed more often on this item; the authors revised wording and the explanations document to improve clarity. Score 0–2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 5: Scientific reasoning (presentation of evidence level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The review should present scientific reasoning—i.e., indicate levels of evidence and reason logically from the cited literature to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the authors appropriately interpret evidence, acknowledge strengths/limitations, and indicate evidence levels where applicable. Anchor definitions/examples provided. Score 0–2. This item assesses the coherence and rigor of argumentation rather than originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 6: Presentation of relevant and appropriate endpoint data
rubrics_metrics.description: The review should present relevant and appropriate endpoint/outcome data (reporting of pertinent results and outcomes from the literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether important endpoints are included and presented appropriately (not selectively reported), and whether data presentation supports conclusions. This item scored relatively low in testing. Score 0–2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the six items is rated 0 (low standard), 1 (intermediate), or 2 (high standard); maximal sum score is 12. The sum score is intended to measure the construct 'quality of a narrative review article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor definitions and examples accompany each item in the 'explanations and instructions' document and should be used for consistent scoring. There are no established cut-offs for quality grades across settings, though the authors note a score of 4 or below indicates very poor quality in their experience. SANRA sum scores showed a modest association with editorial acceptance in one study; use SANRA as one decision aid among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use, feasibility, and rater training
rubrics_metrics.description: SANRA is intended to be simple and brief enough for everyday editorial use and to assist editors, reviewers, readers, and authors; feasibility was confirmed by experienced editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend rater training using the explanations and instructions document and suggest group training sessions. Reliability (ICC) and internal consistency are adequate but not perfect; training reduces disagreement (notably for items 1 and 4). SANRA may complement journal-specific evaluation (e.g., audience, originality) but should not replace those considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations / domains not covered
rubrics_metrics.description: SANRA is a short critical appraisal tool (six items) and is not a reporting guideline; it does not comprehensively cover all facets of review quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly excluded some domains (e.g., originality, quality of tables and figures, and a previously-considered item on writing/accessibility that was deleted due to poor inter-rater reliability). The brevity improves feasibility but restricts content validity; users should be aware of these limitations and not use SANRA as the sole quality metric.
